originalTitle: Almost 75% of A&E staff in UK face violence or aggression daily or weekly
summary: Survey finds long waiting times and overcrowding have made abuse ‘routine’ part of working on hospital frontline
content: Nearly three-quarters of A&E staff experience violence or aggression daily or weekly, according to a survey highlighting the “appalling” abuse of NHS workers. The Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM) said understaffed and overcrowded emergency departments were contributing to increased targeting of medics. In a survey of more than 2,000 workers in the UK, 63% said they had suffered discrimination including racism, sexism and homophobia, while 73% said violence or aggression of all kinds was a daily or weekly occurrence. Almost all (96%) said they had experienced abuse from patients or members of the public. Dr Ian Higginson, the president of the RCEM, said: “No one should go to work fearing or, worse, expecting to be attacked, intimidated or abused. Nor should they lack confidence that their employers have their backs, or that the judicial system will kick in. “Yet that’s the reality faced by the majority of my colleagues in EDs [emergency departments] across the country. They often do not feel safe to care for patients. It is an appalling state of affairs which is contributing towards many people seriously considering whether emergency medicine – or even healthcare in general – is for them.” Senior nurses said in January that abuse of NHS staff had become a national crisis. In the survey, emergency department workers said long waiting times and overcrowding had made violence and aggression a “routine” part of working on the hospital frontline. Staff shortages and corridor care – patients being treated in non-clinical spaces because of overcrowding – were also cited as main reasons behind the abuse. One anonymous resident doctor said: “Working in the ED, you brace yourself for a lot, but nothing truly prepares you for direct, hateful verbal abuse, especially when it’s racially charged.” A senior emergency doctor told the survey they had been kicked in the face by an aggressive patient lying on a trolley. Ministers have pledged to get key waiting times across the NHS back on track before the end of this parliament in 2029. However, the leaders of professional bodies have called for faster action after a series of targets were missed at the end of the financial year in March. The NHS was told to ensure 78% of A&E patients were treated within four hours by March. While it came close to that target – 77.6% of patients were treated within four hours that month – the proportion has since slipped. Higginson called on the government to accelerate its drive to reduce waiting times and overcrowding. “Much has been said by us and other organisations over the years about violence and aggression towards healthcare staff. But the problem seems to be getting worse, not better,” he said. “It’s time for action, time for governments, employers and organisations stand up for NHS staff, and time to ensure that those who intimidate, abuse or assault those who are trying to care for them face meaningful consequences for their actions.” The worsening conditions in A&E would have “devastating” consequences for the workforce if they continued, the RCEM added. Only 4% of those surveyed said they always felt safe working in A&E, while 75% reported short-term stress and anxiety, 40% said they had experienced burnout and 28% long-term stress or anxiety. In January, data obtained by the Guardian revealed that more than 295,000 incidents of physical violence and aggression by patients against staff had been recorded by 212 NHS trusts in England between 2022 and 2025. Hospitals records showed the number of violent incidents, which ranged from violent threats to attempted and actual assaults, had risen from 91,175 in 2022-23 to 104,079 in 2024-25. This was equivalent to about 285 cases being reported every day in the most recent year. A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Any acts of violence, abuse or harassment towards NHS staff are completely unacceptable and will not be tolerated. Everyone working in our national health service has a fundamental right to be safe at work, and it is deeply concerning that so many emergency department staff continue to experience this behaviour. “That is why this government recently introduced new NHS staff standards, which set out the steps that every NHS employer across the country must take to prevent and reduce violence and abuse against their staff and help ensure they can do their jobs safely.”
chineseTitle: 英国近 75% 的急症室工作人员每天或每周都会面临暴力或攻击行为
chineseSummary: 调查发现，漫长的等待时间和过度拥挤使得虐待成为医院前线工作的“常态”
chineseContent: 一项强调 NHS 工作人员遭受“令人震惊”的虐待的调查显示，近四分之三的急症室工作人员每天或每周都会遭受暴力或攻击。英国皇家急诊医学学院（RCEM）表示，急诊科人手不足和人满为患，加剧了针对医务人员的攻击。在对英国 2000 多名工人进行的一项调查中，63% 的人表示他们遭受过包括种族主义、性别歧视和恐同在内的歧视，而 73% 的人表示各种暴力或攻击行为每天或每周都会发生。几乎所有人（96%）表示他们曾遭受过患者或公众的虐待。 RCEM 主席伊恩·希金森 (Ian Higginson) 博士表示：“任何人上班时都不应该害怕，或者更糟糕的是，担心会受到攻击、恐吓或虐待。他们也不应该对雇主的支持或司法系统的介入缺乏信心。“然而，这就是我在全国急诊室的大多数同事所面临的现实。他们常常觉得照顾病人不安全。这种令人震惊的状况促使许多人认真考虑急诊医学——甚至一般的医疗保健——是否适合他们。”高级护士在一月份表示，虐待 NHS 工作人员已成为一场全国性危机。在调查中，急诊科工作人员表示，漫长的等待时间和过度拥挤使得暴力和攻击行为成为医院前线工作的“常规”部分。人员短缺和走廊护理（患者因过度拥挤而在非临床空间接受治疗）也被认为是虐待背后的主要原因。一位不愿透露姓名的住院医生说：“在急诊室工作，你要做好很多准备，但没有什么能真正让你做好面对直接、仇恨性辱骂的准备，尤其是当
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
